title: Chinese researchers solve 3D Ghys conjecture with homegrown AI model

Computer-generated animation shows the Arnold cat map stretching, a classic example of the chaotic Anosov systems at the heart of the 3D Ghys conjecture. /CMG
A Chinese research team has fully proved the 3D Ghys conjecture, a world-class mathematical problem that had baffled the international mathematics community for more than 30 years. It is the first time Chinese scientists have relied on a domestically developed large AI model to crack a problem at this level.
The team, led by Xu Disheng, a professor at the Greater Bay University and a visiting scholar at the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (Shanghai AI Lab), worked with the lab's Intern-S2 science large model to solve the conjecture. The AI took on large-scale, long-chain and highly complex mathematical derivations, while the researchers steered the overall direction and screened out promising lines of reasoning.
After multiple rounds of iterative interaction, the collaboration produced a complete and rigorous proof of the conjecture.
Independent verification was carried out by a Peking University team led by Liu Ruochuan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Professor Dong Bin. Using a self-developed framework and massive parallel computing with AI agents, the team completed formal machine verification of all core theorems and generated hundreds of thousands of lines of verification code, rigorously confirming that the entire proof is logically complete, gap-free and fully valid.
First proposed in 1995 by French mathematician Étienne Ghys, the conjecture has long stood as a central unsolved problem in complex dynamics, with extreme reasoning difficulty. Its real-number counterpart remains an open problem worldwide and is regarded as a key benchmark for measuring advanced mathematical reasoning ability.
The paper has been released on an international preprint platform, and the verification code has been fully open-sourced.

report.summary: Chinese researchers used the homegrown Intern-S2 AI model to prove the 3D Ghys conjecture, a 30-year-old complex dynamics problem, with independent formal verification and open-sourced code.
report.background: The 3D Ghys conjecture was proposed in 1995 by French mathematician Étienne Ghys and became a central open problem in complex dynamics, especially around chaotic Anosov systems. Its real-number counterpart remains unsolved and is widely used as a benchmark for advanced mathematical reasoning. The problem is notable not only for its difficulty but for requiring long, highly coupled derivations that are hard to check by hand. The reported proof comes from a collaboration led by Xu Disheng of Greater Bay University and Shanghai AI Lab, using the lab's domestically developed Intern-S2 science large model. The work reflects a broader push to apply specialized AI models to frontier science, and China's interest in building homegrown AI capabilities. Independent verification by a Peking University team, plus open-sourcing of verification code, adds weight to the claim.
key_points: A Chinese team says it has fully proved the 3D Ghys conjecture, an open mathematics problem from 1995. The team was led by Xu Disheng of Greater Bay University and Shanghai AI Lab. It is described as the first time Chinese scientists have used a domestically developed large AI model to crack a problem at this level.

The AI model, Intern-S2, handled large-scale, long-chain and highly complex mathematical derivations. Researchers set the overall direction and screened promising lines of reasoning. Through multiple rounds of interaction, the human-AI collaboration produced a complete and rigorous proof. This shows a workflow where AI does heavy derivation while humans provide judgment and steering.

An independent Peking University team led by Liu Ruochuan and Dong Bin checked the proof. It used a self-developed framework and massive parallel computing with AI agents to formally verify all core theorems. The team generated hundreds of thousands of lines of verification code and confirmed the proof is logically complete, gap-free and valid.

The paper has been released on an international preprint platform, and the verification code has been fully open-sourced. That matters because other researchers can inspect, reproduce and build on the result. Open verification code also helps distinguish a genuine machine-checked proof from a persuasive but incomplete argument.

The 3D Ghys conjecture is a central problem in complex dynamics. Its real-number counterpart remains open and is seen as a benchmark for advanced mathematical reasoning. Solving the 3D case with AI therefore signals progress not just in mathematics but in measuring and improving AI's rigorous reasoning ability.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result is a strong signal that domain-specialized science models can contribute to frontier mathematics when paired with human direction and formal verification. It shifts attention from raw model scale toward reliable workflows: iterative human-AI collaboration, proof assistants, and machine-checkable outputs. For developers, the open-sourced verification code and preprint provide concrete artifacts for studying AI-assisted theorem proving and building agent-based formal math pipelines. For regular users, the effect is indirect: faster scientific progress and stronger trust in AI outputs that can be mechanically checked, rather than an immediate consumer product. The caveat is that one high-profile proof does not mean AI can independently solve open problems; human framing, screening and verification remain essential.
report.tools: Watch Shanghai AI Lab's Intern-S2 science model and the open-sourced verification code from this work. For hands-on follow-up, explore formal proof assistants such as Lean, Coq and Isabelle, and AI-agent theorem-proving frameworks that connect language models to machine-checkable proofs. The preprint and code repository are the best starting points for reproducibility and further experiments.
